senses.sense: The hidden things and powers of natural things, which true philosophers and skilled physicians search out, understand and imitate; finding them out is called the chief temporal thing and the end of Physick, and the cheats are called unworthy of them.

evidence.quote: men skill'd in the secrets of Nature
as ignorant and unworthy of the mysteries of God, and the secrets of Nature
they doe at last attaine not onely to understand, but also really to imitate the greatest mysteries and secrets of Nature
in temporalls the chiefest thing is to find out the secrets of Nature
the end of Phisick is not to scrape up money, but to discover the secrets of Nature
not onely to come all the desired Secrets of Nature

senses.sense: Cheats among the pretended physicians (the spurious Theophrasteans of OPEN.11), who carry their impostures about the country and falsely accuse innocent men.

evidence.quote: those base Impostors which deserve to be made Mine-diggers
are wont not only falsly to accuse many innocent men of upright, vertuous and blamelesse life

senses.sense: Pretenders to the chief Medicine of the philosophers, who cheat great men with golden promises; some have got the Ferment prepared by others but cannot multiply it for want of the principle. The 'transmutatory virtue' given them is the author's irony: it turns rich men poor (Interpreted).

evidence.quote: some Impostors in our age who right or wrong by unlawfull means having got the most true Phylosophycall Ferment or Leaven
by the golden promises of circumforaneous, vitious, and most lying Impostors
of which those Phylosophists and Imposters are altogether destitute
this efficacious transmutatory virtue of these Impostors, which makes wise men fools, strong men weak, rich men poor

senses.sense: Students named after Theophrastus who contemplate the workmanship of Nature, the heavens and sublunary bodies, and come to understand and imitate its secrets. That these are the genuine kind is inferred from the text setting 'also false and lying Theophrasteans' apart from them.

evidence.quote: Theophrasteans contemplate and admire the workmanship of Nature throughout this mighty frame of the whole Creation
There are also false and lying Theophrasteans prophaning by their avarice and timerity that Divine Physick

senses.sense: False, spurious or 'adulterous' Theophrasteans: wandering cheats who claim to use Theophrastus his medicines, prepare remedies unlawfully and put the sick in danger.

evidence.quote: As for the spurious and adulterous Theophrasteans (the worst and wickedest sort of men)
who under disguised names vaunt and vapour that they make use of Theophrastus his medicines
these circumforaneous and adulterous Theophrasteans, with their unlawfully prepared Remedies

senses.sense: Physicians of the received school named after Galen, who reason by qualities (hot, cold, bitter) and, the margin says, know nothing of Astral cures; one milder part of them is said to hold back from professing the truth for fear.

evidence.quote: By this Art only the Galenists may make good their Axioms, who affirm that all bitter things are hot
The Galenists doe know nothing of these Astral cures, which the grave experienced Physitians do well understand.
But the more single and subtle part of the Galenists, who like Nicodemus are of a milder temper
Hippocrates wrote many things, which most Galenists reject at this day
doe sometime exceed many Galenists in many great and perilous diseases

senses.sense: Belief held without tested truth, set against the truth found by experiment; named with Scorne as a hindrance ('let') of learning, cast away by those who come to the truth, and said in the margin to rule the world.

evidence.quote: having first cast away Opinion and Scorne the lets of learning
The world is ruled by Opinion.
not fallacious opinions
but the truth it self so long desired, by many experiments most certainly found out and known

senses.sense: Nature spoken of as a book, second after the book of Grace: Physick is written in it, in Heaven and Earth, every region is a leaf of it, and it is to be read practically and experimentally; the margin says only the physician who follows the mind of Paracelsus can open it.

evidence.quote: Physick is written in the book of Nature (1) in Heaven and Earth, and may there be read & found out by Chyromancy and phisiognomy
desireth chiefly to turn over the BOOK of NATURE (in which every region is a leaf) not profunctorily & superficially, but practically and experimentally
And next after the great book of Grace, wherein the eternall health of our soules consisteth, more diligently to pry into that other also of Nature
that Physitian that walketh according to the mind of Paracelsus is onely able to open the Book of Nature

senses.sense: The art, study and profession of healing.

evidence.quote: in the practice of Physick
the Titles and Honours of Philosophy and Phisick
thrust themselves into the profession of Physick with unwashen hands

senses.sense: Healing as God's gift: the created and incarnate Mercy of God, set in things beside his Justice, which is the disease and venom.

evidence.quote: Physick is nothing else but the created and incarnate Mercy of our Heavenly Father
the Mercy of God is the Physick in Nature and in all things
Physick is a favour given of God

senses.sense: The healing power hidden in things, wrapped in coverings and to be separated from them; a Spirit, not a body, discerned only by the wise man.

evidence.quote: the true medicine (or Physick) is wrapt up in rindes, barks, matrixes, receptacles, husks, garment and cottages
Physick is a Spirit (not a body) which the Magician or wise man only can discerne

senses.sense: The work of curing itself: refreshing the strength and Balsom and removing the impurities that cause diseases.

evidence.quote: For Physick is nothing else but an opposition of those things that are desired, to wit, a refreshing of the strength and Balsom, and a removing of superfluityes or impurities that cause diseases

senses.sense: An author the text cites and follows as an authority in Physick and philosophy, whose due place in practice and preparations it claims; the margin says only the physician who follows his mind can open the Book of Nature, and gives words of his a sense of his own ('the Salt of Paracelsus').

evidence.quote: as you may find in the Sage and deep Phylosophy of Paracelsus
give place to Paracelsus according to his desert in practice and preparations
that Physitian that walketh according to the mind of Paracelsus is onely able to open the Book of Nature
When Paracelsus saith that like preserve their like, and are destroyed by their contraryes
All Terresterity is the Salt of Paracelsus.

senses.sense: Man, and his body, as the small copy of the great world: one and the same with it in all things, preserved, nourished and cured by it.

evidence.quote: the little World Man
For that little world Man is one and the same in all things with his-Parant, the great world
Man is therefore called a Microcosm or little world, because the whole world preserveth, nourisheth and cureth him
in the little world, the body, there lurketh perpetuall strife
by destroying the frame of the little world and taking away our life
the Harmony between the great and little world

senses.sense: The active, healing or harmful power in a thing, which the text sets apart from its quality (hot, cold): Nature itself is a vertue, not a quality, and is helped by vertues; without vertue a quality is dead.

evidence.quote: Nature is not a quality but a vertue
for without vertue the quallity is dead and wholly accidentall
by the Specifick venemous vertue of the Opium
How, and with what Vertue, Physick worketh upon Mans body and cureth his Diseases.
before they can impart their hidden and restrained vertues
by a specifick and Harmonicall vertue serve to cure and comfort the heart
the Naturall innate vertue of things that grow of the Earth, the Celestiall influence causing that vertue

senses.sense: Moral goodness, which draws envy.

evidence.quote: But virtue can never be found without the marks and wounds of envy

senses.sense: The physician as servant of Nature and of God, who separates and administers what he received, and is not Nature's master.

evidence.quote: The Duty of Natures Minister, the Physitian.
A true Phisitian should be the minister, not a master to Nature
Nature hath commanded the Physitians to be ministers, and to seperate, not masters to compose
But to the Physitian who is the obedient Minister of God and Nature
What manner of Phisitian that Phisick doth require for its Minister.

senses.sense: Death called God's servant, waiting on the war within man.

evidence.quote: Death Gods minister expecteth our intestine war.

senses.sense: The Physick the author sets out to treat: the gift of God alone, not learned from the Heathens, covered in bark and rind and to be got out and prepared by Fire; what he says he longed to find.

evidence.quote: CHAP. I. Of the True Physick.
THE true Physick whereof by the Devine assistance I intend here to treat, is the mear gift of the most high God
it is not to be sought for or learned from the Heathens, but from God alone
How the True Physick, which is covered bark and rind, is to be got out, and rightly prepared by Fire.
but with an exceeding love to find out the True Physick

senses.sense: True Physick as a branch of knowledge named beside Astronomy and Chymistry, needed to understand Theophrastus his preparations.

evidence.quote: which cannot be understood without true Physick

senses.sense: Metals not subject to corruption, in which above all God has written in sublunary things, and whose Spirits free man's body from corruption; against those who deny their likeness to man's body the author answers that mineral, vegetable and animal seed have one origin. The lines do not name which metals these are.

evidence.quote: upon which God hath written with his own sacred finger in sublunary things, but especially in perfect Mettalls
as the Spirits of perfect mettalls doe, which are not subject to corruptions
let them know that the Animall, Vegetable and Minerall sperm or seed have but one rise or originall

senses.sense: The metal as a medicine, whose powers would show if it were rightly refined and made potable; set down for the heart and as thickening Mercury.

evidence.quote: There is no question to be made but the Gold would discover most Divine actions if it were rightly refined
so as to make solid and massy Gold potable, that it may be drunk
for the heart, Gold, Pearles, Saffron
Gold thickneth the too much sublimation of Mercury.
As he that hath much Gold may know nothing of its medicinall vertue.

senses.sense: Gold as wealth and money; the aside in CH2.5 sets it beside gold the medicine, and the author says he did not seek to make Gold.

evidence.quote: Gold (which cheareth up the Spirits when a man hath enough of it in his purse)
not to the end that I might make Gold and Silver

senses.sense: The name the margin gives to 'this Physicall essence in Phisick'; the note does not say further what that essence is.

evidence.quote: This Physicall essence in Phisick is called Gold.
